title: Scored against its own target, the unadjusted comparison ranked best; against a declared target it ranked worst
question: Does scoring each method against its own implicit target give the same method ranking as scoring against a declared decision target, across a menu of targets and with correct or misspecified second-stage transport?
design: Anchored binary-outcome comparison with individual data on A versus C and published B versus C; three declared targets, B sharing A's modification or not; Bucher, MAIC, STC and two-stage STC; mismatch term exact, estimation term from 1000 replicates per cell, 6 cells.
answer: No. The method with the lowest RMSE against its own implicit target differed from the one with the lowest RMSE against the declared decision target in 5 of 6 cells. The unadjusted Bucher comparison, scored against the mixture of populations it estimates, won the native metric everywhere because it has the least variance, and was biased by 0.13 to 0.25 against the declared target in five cells. When the comparator's modification differed from the individual-data treatment's, methods native to the comparator trial's population missed a declared target one covariate SD away by 0.11, and a two-stage transport assuming shared modification did not remove it.
findings: Target mismatch (exact): 0 to 0.003 with shared modification; up to 0.11 for MAIC and STC and 0.25 for Bucher without it.
Among adjusted methods RMSE differences were within 0.03 against a sampling SD of about 0.25, so their order is not resolved at 300 per arm.
Two-stage STC removed the mismatch under shared modification and matched MAIC's bias when it failed.
not_answered: Three declared targets, one covariate, one sample size, exact target moments, four methods; no ML-NMR or ML-UMR. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Marginal log odds ratio B versus A in a declared target population
methods_compared: two-stage STC to the declared target
n_sim: 1000 per cell, 6 cells; mismatch term by quadrature
